sessions.setting: Bayou Table restaurant kitchen, after the Wednesday dinner rush

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: That was a crazy service tonight. Forty-two covers on a Wednesday.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Tell me about it. I ran out of bread pudding by eight o'clock. The cardamom-praline one.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Priya, that bread pudding is single-handedly keeping Bayou Table on the map. Didn't Eater New Orleans just feature it?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: They did, yeah. Which is why everyone's ordering it now. I need to start doubling the batch. How's the cookbook coming along, by the way?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Slowly. I've been collecting recipes from the club for 'Frenchmen Street Kitchen,' but organizing them into chapters is harder than I thought.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: You should include the dessert section from me and Rosa. Our pastry collaborations have been some of the best club nights.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Oh, definitely. Your stuff is going in there. I just need to test everything one more time. You know me, head chef brain — everything has to be perfect.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Perfectionist. That's why Magazine Street keeps filling up every night.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Speaking of which, I need to finalize the spring menu tomorrow. Want to brainstorm dessert pairings before we leave?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Sure. Let me just finish cleaning my station. Give me ten minutes.

sessions.setting: Marcus's home kitchen on Frenchmen Street, Wednesday Night Cooking Club

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Marcus, I brought over a big batch of agua de jamaica. Should I set it up on the counter?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Absolutely. Ever since you introduced that to the club, it's basically become our official drink. I don't think anyone touches anything else on Wednesdays anymore.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: I'll take a glass right now, baby. Let me just get my grandmother's pot set up first. Can't cook without it.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Lorraine, you bring that cast-iron pot every single week. It must weigh a ton.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Thirty pounds, but it's seasoned with six generations of love. I'm the oldest one in this club, and this pot's even older than me.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: That pot has made some of the best food I've ever tasted. Glad you only have to walk it next door, Rosa. Perks of us being neighbors.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Right? I literally walked over here in my slippers tonight. Living next door to the guy who founded the cooking club has its advantages.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I started this whole thing back in January 2023, and honestly, having you right next door is why you were my first recruit.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Well, I'm glad you invited me too. Now pour me some of that jamaica, Rosa, and let's get cooking. What are we making tonight?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I was thinking we do a roux-off. Everyone makes their roux, and we compare.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Oh, this should be fun. Lorraine, your roux is legendary.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Honey, I've been stirring roux since before you were born. Let's see what you've got.

sessions.setting: Swan River Yoga studio on Magazine Street, before morning class

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Good morning, Lorraine! You beat me here again.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: I've been getting here by quarter to seven every morning this week. My body just wakes up early. Seventh Ward habits — my family's been in this city for six generations, and we've always been early risers.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Six generations in New Orleans? That's incredible. I've only been here since 2016. I came from Chennai for culinary school — the New Orleans Culinary and Hospitality Institute.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: And look at you now, pastry chef at one of the best restaurants in town. Chennai to New Orleans is quite a journey, baby.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: It really is. Some mornings when I'm biking from my place on Esplanade Avenue to the studio here, I still pinch myself. Three blocks from the French Quarter and I'm living in a shotgun house. It feels like a dream.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Esplanade is beautiful. I love that stretch near the Quarter. You settled in nicely.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I have. This yoga class helps so much. Every weekday at seven, rain or shine. It keeps me centered before the chaos of the pastry kitchen.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Same for me, honey. After twenty-five years of nursing, my back needs this. Alright, looks like they're opening the doors. Ready?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Let's do it. Want to grab coffee after?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Always.

sessions.setting: Marcus's backyard on Frenchmen Street, testing fusion recipes

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Alright, Hideo, the smoker's been going for about six hours now. This tasso ham should be ready soon.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: You built this smoker yourself, right? It's impressive.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Yeah, custom-built. I smoke all my own tasso back here. It's one of those things where you just can't get the flavor right from a store. So what are you thinking for the fusion dish tonight?

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: I brought fresh dashi. I make it from scratch every morning at Kura — dried bonito flakes and kombu seaweed. I was thinking we fold the tasso into a dashi broth base and create something like a Cajun ramen.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Cajun ramen. Man, this is why we're the best cooking partners in the club. Nobody else is doing Cajun-Japanese fusion like us.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: That's what drew me to New Orleans in the first place. When I moved here in 2019, I wanted to explore the overlap between Japanese and Creole seafood traditions. And then I met you, and it all came together.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I remember that first club night when you showed up. You brought that miso butter and put it on my crawfish. I was like, this man is a genius.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: And you showed me what a real roux tastes like. So, should we try the tasso-dashi broth? I'm thinking we serve it over thick noodles with poached Gulf shrimp.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Let's do it. I'll pull the tasso off the smoker and we can start building the broth.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Perfect. This could be the centerpiece of next week's club night.

sessions.setting: Rosa's Honda CR-V, driving home from the Seventh Ward

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Thanks for waiting, Hideo. Parent conferences ran long today. Fourth graders — you'd think they'd be easy, but the parents have so many questions.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: No problem at all. I really appreciate you driving me. Six months without my car is killing me.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: That Subaru of yours has been in the shop forever. What's wrong with it again?

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Engine issue. The silver Outback is basically living at the mechanic's at this point. They keep finding new problems.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: That's awful. Well, carpooling works out anyway. William Frantz Elementary isn't far from Kura, so the route makes sense.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: It does. And honestly, I enjoy the company. Is that a Virgen de Guadalupe air freshener?

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Yes! My mother gave it to me years ago. This old white CR-V has seen better days, but that air freshener stays.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: I like it. It smells nice too. Like lavender.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: It is lavender. So how was the lunch rush at Kura today?

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Busy. We had a big group come in for a birthday. I made about forty pieces of nigiri. My hands are tired.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: You need a hand massage. I know a good place on Magazine Street.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Maybe after my car's fixed and I can actually drive myself there.

sessions.setting: Marcus's home kitchen, Wednesday Night Cooking Club, working on desserts

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Rosa, I picked up some jaggery from the Indian grocery on Broad Street. I was thinking we could try it in tonight's dessert.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Jaggery? Is that the unrefined cane sugar you're always talking about?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Yes! It's my favorite ingredient to work with. It has this deep, almost caramelly flavor. I think it would be incredible in a praline.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Oh, interesting. You know, I was going to suggest we do a chocolate component tonight. I have some chocolate from Oaxaca that I use in my mole negro.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Your mole negro! That recipe is insane. Seven ingredients, three days of work. That chocolate must be special.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: It is. My family's been using it for generations. But we could use it in a pastry context too. You're the expert — you're my cooking partner for a reason.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: And you're mine. Desserts and pastries are our thing in this club. Remember that masala chai king cake we did for King Cake Festival?

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Second place! That was amazing. I still can't believe we almost won.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Almost. Next year, we'll take first. So what do you think — jaggery-Oaxacan chocolate truffles?

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Let's do it. I'll melt the chocolate and you handle the jaggery reduction.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Deal. This is why Wednesday nights are the best night of the week.

sessions.setting: Marcus's kitchen after cooking club, everyone else has left

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Lorraine, can I ask you something? That roux you made tonight — it was perfect. Every time. How do you do it?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Baby, I taught you how to make proper Creole roux when you first moved to New Orleans. You've gotten good, but you still rush it.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I know, I know. CIA trained me to be efficient. When I graduated from the Culinary Institute of America in 2010, everything was about speed and precision.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Hyde Park teaches you technique. New Orleans teaches you patience. Those are two different things.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: That's true. I grew up in Lafayette watching my grandmother at her boudin stand, and even she said I was always in a hurry.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Your grandmother knew. Good food takes time. My red beans and rice — I use pickled pork from Langenstein's and a secret blend of seven spices. That pot simmers for hours.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Your red beans are the best I've ever had. Bar none.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Thank you, baby. Jerome always says the same thing. That man eats them every Monday without fail.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: How is Jerome doing? Still building furniture?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Oh yes. Retired from the fire department, and now he's in the garage every day making custom pieces. He just finished a dining table from reclaimed cypress. Beautiful work.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I need to commission something from him. My kitchen table is falling apart.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Just call him. He'd love to make something for you.

sessions.setting: Bayou Table restaurant, lunch prep break

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Marcus, I just got a call about the food festival. They want us both back for panels this year.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Oh nice! After that crawfish boil masterclass I taught there earlier this month, they want more?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Apparently you were a hit. I still remember catering desserts for that 300-person Mardi Gras ball in February. The Krewe of Muses one. That nearly killed me.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Three hundred people! That's insane. How did you even manage that?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I didn't sleep for two days. But it was worth it. Lots of new connections. Speaking of the festival — remember your gumbo competition win last year?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: The duck and andouille gumbo at the New Orleans Gumbo Festival? Yeah, that was a good day.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: A good day? You won the whole thing. I was so proud. Hey, completely different topic — I started reading 'Tartine Bread' again. Chad Robertson's approach to fermentation is giving me ideas.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: For the restaurant or the club?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Both, honestly. I want to do a naturally leavened dessert bread with South Indian spices. Oh, and I've been meaning to ask — can we do more of the Cajun French lessons? I'm picking it up, but slowly.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Mais oui! You already speak Tamil, Hindi, and English. Adding Cajun French to that is impressive.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Three languages makes the fourth easier, or so they say. Alright, break's over. Back to the pastry station.

sessions.setting: Lorraine's house on North Claiborne Avenue, dropping off groceries

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Lorraine, I brought the kombu seaweed you asked for. And some extra bonito flakes.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Thank you, sweetheart. Come in, come in. The grandchildren are here — it's Friday, so I'm babysitting all four of them.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Four grandkids every Friday? That's a workout.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: It is, but I love it. They're in the backyard right now, playing in the garden. Jerome built me these beautiful raised beds, and I grow all my herbs there — basil, thyme, oregano, bay laurel.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: That's wonderful. Yuki was just saying we should start an herb garden. She keeps talking about how her cousin Jerome has such a green thumb.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Well, Jerome and Yuki are first cousins, so the family connection runs deep. Which makes you and me cousins by marriage, Hideo. Family helps family.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Exactly. And Yuki loves visiting you. She says your house always smells incredible.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: That's the herbs and the roux, baby. Now, tell me about this wife of yours. How's her teaching going at Tulane?

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: She's doing well. The Japanese language classes are popular this semester. Full enrollment.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Good for her. Now, do you want to stay for dinner? I'm making gumbo with the grandkids tonight.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: I'd love to, but I promised Rosa I'd be ready for our carpool at seven tomorrow morning. Rain check?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Anytime, baby. You're family.

sessions.setting: Marcus's home kitchen, Wednesday Night Cooking Club

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Marcus, I brought a bag of habaneros from my garden. Fresh off the plant this morning.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Habaneros! Rosa, your backyard pepper garden is out of control. What else are you growing this year?

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Habaneros, serranos, and guajillos. Same as always. They love the Frenchmen Street soil.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Can I take some serranos? I want to try them in a praline recipe I'm developing. I'm working on a South Indian-inspired praline line to sell at the French Market.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Take as many as you want! That sounds amazing. Oh, and Sofia sends her love, Priya. She loved those cardamom cookies you sent home last week.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Aw, how old is Sofia now? Sixteen?

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Sixteen, yes. Miguel is thirteen and Luna is nine. They're growing up too fast.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I know the feeling. Celine is twelve now, and she's already telling me my cooking is 'mid.' Can you believe that? My own daughter.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Kids these days. What school is she at?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Lusher Charter School. She loves it. Hey, we should talk about tonight's main — I'm doing my 48-hour slow-cooked pork shoulder with cane syrup glaze. It's been going since Monday.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Oh, that's your specialty! The one that takes two full days?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Two days of low and slow. Trust me, it's worth the wait. Grab a plate.

sessions.setting: Coffee shop near Swan River Yoga after morning class

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: That was a tough class today. My shoulders are going to be sore tomorrow.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Mine too. But worth it. Hey, I wanted to show you something. Look at this little face.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Oh! Is that the cat you adopted?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Yes! Masala. I adopted her from the Louisiana SPCA back in March. She's a tabby and she's already the queen of my shotgun house.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Masala! What a perfect name for a chef's cat. She's beautiful.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: She sits on the counter while I test recipes. Which reminds me — Lorraine, you know how I've been talking about opening my own bakery?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: In Bywater, right? The Indo-Creole pastry place? Baby, I think about that all the time. You'd be amazing.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: That's the dream. Indo-Creole pastries. I just need to save up more. The praline line at the French Market is supposed to help with that.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: You know who you should read? Leah Chase. Her cookbook — 'Leah Chase: The Queen of Creole Cuisine' — that's my bible. That woman built an empire from a kitchen.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I'll pick it up. You've mentioned her before. You were a nurse for how long before you retired?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Twenty-five years at Ochsner Medical Center. Cardiac unit, registered nurse. I retired in 2022, and I haven't looked back. Cooking full-time is what I was always meant to do.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: That's inspiring, honestly. From nursing to the kitchen. Alright, I need to get going. I'm parked on Magazine — the red Kia Soul with the bumper sticker.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: 'Bakers Gonna Bake'! I love that thing. Drive safe, honey.

sessions.setting: Marcus's home kitchen, Wednesday Night Cooking Club

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Hideo, what's in that case you brought tonight?

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: My good knives. I import them directly from a bladesmith in Sakai, Japan. This set is worth over five thousand dollars.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Lord have mercy. Five thousand dollars for knives?

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: They're hand-forged. Each one takes weeks to make. I've been collecting them since my training days. I spent seven years at a sushi restaurant in Tsukiji, Tokyo, after growing up in Osaka. Knives are everything in Japanese cuisine.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I respect that. I've got my own kind of collection — over 200 hot sauce bottles in the garage. Organized by Scoville rating.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Marcus, that is the most you thing I've ever heard. Two hundred hot sauces!

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: What? I need options. Different sauces for different dishes.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: You should try Japanese yuzu kosho. It would fit right in your collection. Speaking of fusion, I wanted to tell you both — the miso-crawfish roll I created became the best-selling item at Kura this year.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: The miso-crawfish roll! I had that last month. Hideo, it was magnifique. See, I'm practicing my French.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Lorraine, you speak Louisiana Creole French, right? That's the real deal.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Creole French and English, baby. And I can read standard French too. My family kept the language alive all these generations.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Alright, enough talking. Hideo, let's see what those five-thousand-dollar knives can do. We're breaking down a whole redfish tonight.

sessions.setting: Marcus's home kitchen, Wednesday Night Cooking Club ladies' night theme

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Ladies, it's just us three tonight. Marcus and Hideo are doing some fishing thing.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Perfect. We can actually cook without Marcus hovering over everyone's pot. So, what are we making?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: My mom just sent me a fresh batch of homemade curry powder from Chennai. She ships it every three months by international post. I was thinking we try it in something.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Your mother sends you curry powder from India? That's love right there.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Lakshmi doesn't mess around. She packs it in triple-sealed bags. It's incredible stuff.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Let's use it! I can translate the recipe card if it's in English. I only speak Spanish and English, but I'm good at figuring out recipes.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Rosa, speaking of your talents — didn't you win Teacher of the Year last year?

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: I did! At William Frantz Elementary, 2023. It was such an honor. Being able to translate for Spanish-speaking parents at the school was a big part of why they nominated me.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: You deserve it. You do so much for that community.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: She really does. Now, I made seafood gumbo with okra this Monday, like I always do, and I delivered portions to three elderly neighbors on my street. But I saved some for tonight.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Lorraine, you are the sweetest person alive. My daughter Sofia keeps saying she wants to be like you when she grows up. Actually, no — Sofia's current obsession is 'My Mexico City Kitchen' by Gabriela Camara. She wants to go to culinary school.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Like mother, like daughter. Alright, let's get cooking. Curry gumbo fusion, anyone?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Now you're speaking my language.

sessions.setting: Marcus's home kitchen and backyard, Wednesday Night Cooking Club — Juneteenth celebration

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Alright, everybody listen up! Tonight is special. I've organized a Juneteenth celebration, and we're doing a traditional Creole feast. I've got forty people coming.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Forty people? Lorraine, my kitchen is big, but not that big. Good thing I set up tables in the backyard. I had to move my truck to make room. That F-150 is huge.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: The black one with the ROUX-BOY license plate? I saw it parked down the street.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: That's the one. Custom plate. I'm proud of it.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: I came straight from Zumba at the YMCA on St. Charles. My legs are jelly, but I'm here to help.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Rosa, thank you, baby. Everyone's pitching in. Hideo, did you bring the fish?

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: I brought redfish and speckled trout. Caught them myself in the Bienvenue Triangle marsh on Sunday. I go fishing there every other Sunday morning.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Fresh Gulf fish for a Juneteenth feast. Perfect.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I brought desserts from my Saturday baking class at the Treme Community Center. The students helped me make pralines and bread pudding.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Priya, you teach those baking classes every Saturday? That's wonderful.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Every Saturday morning. The kids are getting really good.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Alright, team. Let's make this the best Juneteenth celebration this club has ever seen. Lorraine, you're in charge. What do you need from us?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: I need Marcus on the grill, Hideo on the fish, Priya on desserts, and Rosa, help me with the sides. Let's feed forty people tonight.

sessions.setting: Marcus's home kitchen, after cooking club, everyone else has left

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Marcus, I wanted to tell you — I'm going to Oaxaca next week. My mother and I are visiting my aunt Elena to learn traditional mole recipes.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Oaxaca! That's incredible, Rosa. How long will you be gone?

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: About two weeks in July. Carlos is going to hold down the fort with the kids. He's got a tough schedule at Avondale Shipyard, but he'll manage.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Carlos is a welder there, right? That's hard work.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: He is. Forty hours a week minimum, often more. But he wants me to go. He knows how important this is. My aunt Elena's mole recipes go back generations.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Bring back recipes for the club. And for the cookbook.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: I will. Oh, and Sofia wants me to find a culinary school program in Oaxaca for her to look at. My sixteen-year-old is dead set on being a chef. She already helps me prep tamale filling on weekends.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: That's amazing. She could be the next great Mexican-American chef. Speaking of family, I need to call my dad this weekend. Jean-Pierre still makes boudin at the family stand in Lafayette every Saturday.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Your father is still running the stand? That's dedication.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Every single Saturday. Rain or shine. Same spot my grandmother had. It's a family thing. Hey, do you want a ride in the morning? I'm heading out for my run early.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Your morning run? What time?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Five-thirty AM. Three miles along the Mississippi River levee. Every morning.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: You're insane. No, I do not want a ride at five-thirty in the morning. I'll see you next Wednesday, neighbor.

sessions.setting: Marcus's home kitchen, Wednesday Night Cooking Club — Hideo's sashimi workshop

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Okay, everyone, tonight I'm teaching sashimi knife skills. I brought yellowfin tuna straight from the Gulf.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: This is going to be good. Show us what you've got.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: First rule — the knife does the work, not your arm. You guide it. I also brought my homemade rice vinegar. I ferment it in ceramic crocks that I brought from Osaka. It takes months.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: You ferment your own vinegar? Hideo, that's impressive. Gracias for teaching us.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: De nada, Rosa. See, I've been picking up conversational Spanish from you during our carpool rides.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: You're getting good! We'll have you fluent by December.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Hideo, before we start, I have news. I won the praline category at the Creole Tomato Festival!

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Lorraine! Congratulations! Which praline was it?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: My bourbon-pecan pralines. The judges said they were the best they'd ever tasted.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: That's amazing, Lorraine. We need to celebrate. Priya, didn't you have good news too?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Oh, yeah! I ran my first 10K — the Crescent City Classic back in April. Finished in 58 minutes.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Fifty-eight minutes! Baby, that's fast.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I was shocked, honestly. All that yoga is paying off.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Congratulations to both of you. Now, let's focus. Everyone pick up a knife, and I'll show you the first cut. This is called the hirazukuri — a flat slice for sashimi.

sessions.setting: Lorraine's house on North Claiborne Avenue, afternoon visit

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Hideo, come sit down. I just got back from WWNO. They interviewed me about Creole food traditions for public radio!

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Public radio! Lorraine, that's amazing. When does it air?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Next month sometime. They want to do a whole segment on generational Creole cooking. I talked about my grandmother's recipes, the cooking club, everything.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: You represent this city's food culture so well. Everyone at the club looks up to you.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Oh, stop. Now, speaking of the club — my granddaughter Amara has been asking to join. She's eight, and she's already learning to make biscuits.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: That's wonderful! Kenji would love that. My son is only three, but he's already fascinated by food. He goes to the same preschool as Marcus's niece, you know.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Small world. New Orleans is like that — everyone's connected. How's the commute from Bywater with your car situation?

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: It's not bad. I live on Chartres Street in a duplex. Rosa's been driving me, which is great, but I miss having my own car.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Well, you're welcome to borrow Big Mama anytime.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Big Mama?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: My gold Cadillac Escalade. 2017. I call her Big Mama. She rides smooth.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: A gold Escalade named Big Mama. Lorraine, you are one of a kind.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: I know, baby. Now sit down and have some gumbo. I made a fresh batch this morning.

sessions.setting: Marcus's home kitchen, Wednesday Night Cooking Club, post-hurricane gathering

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I'm glad everyone's safe after Hurricane Francine. That was scary.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Is everyone's house okay?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: We lost some shingles, but Jerome patched it up. How about you, Marcus?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: My house is fine, but I've been busy. I donated 500 meals to the St. Bernard Project this week for hurricane relief.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Five hundred meals? Marcus, that's incredible.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: It's the least I could do. A lot of people lost everything. My left thumb is still bothering me, though — remember when I broke it shucking oysters at that charity event last September? It took four weeks in a splint, and it still aches when I cook for too long.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: You need to take it easy. I know the feeling — I've been going nonstop too. On a happier note, I got some good news. I won Best Fusion Dish at the New Orleans Wine and Food Experience.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Hideo! Which dish?

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: The shiso-debris po'boy. And I also placed third at the Louisiana Seafood Cook-Off with my Japanese-style grilled oysters.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Two awards! We need to throw you a party.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Seriously. That's amazing. Oh, I wanted to mention — I'm going to Chennai for Diwali in November. Well, last time I went was in 2023, and I brought back 10 kilograms of spices. This time I'm planning to bring even more.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Ten kilos of spices? How did you even get that through customs?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Very carefully. It's worth it, though. Those spices lasted almost the whole year.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Bring some back for the club. We can do another fusion night.

sessions.setting: Tremé Community Center, after Priya's baking class

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Thank you both for coming to help at the bake sale today. We raised $1,800!

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: And I donated 200 pralines. But it was worth it. The Tremé Community Center does so much for this neighborhood.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: I baked 150 conchas for the fundraiser at my school last month. That one raised $2,400 for new playground equipment at William Frantz. It feels good to give back.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: That's what cooking is for, baby. Feeding people. Rosa, aren't you the one who makes all those tamales for the holiday sale too?

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Three hundred tamales every December! All the proceeds from the cooking club's holiday sale go to Second Harvest Food Bank. It's a lot of work, but Carlos and the kids help.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Three hundred tamales. I don't know how you do it.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Sofia does most of the filling now. She's getting really fast. Oh, Lorraine — I heard you're planning something big?

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: I am! I'm going to Paris in October. Two weeks at Le Cordon Bleu for a French pastry course.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Le Cordon Bleu! Lorraine, that's a dream. I'm so jealous.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: It's something I've wanted to do my whole life. Jerome surprised me with the trip for our anniversary.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: That man is a treasure. Oh, by the way — Hideo was telling me during our carpool that he visited his parents in Osaka during Golden Week in May. He said the food there is on another level.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I believe it. I always come back from Chennai inspired too. Travel changes everything.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: That's exactly why I'm going. You're never too old to learn.

sessions.setting: Marcus's home kitchen, Wednesday Night Cooking Club, planning holiday events

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: Alright, let's plan our fall events. We've got a lot coming up.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: I want to do a Dia de los Muertos celebration in November. I'll build an ofrenda with photos and marigolds. It's the one tradition I brought with me when I moved from Veracruz twenty years ago, and I want to share it with the club.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: Twenty years ago? That's when you came to New Orleans?

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: 2004, right after Carlos and I got married. He was already working here, so Veracruz to New Orleans was the move. Best decision of my life.

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: I love that. And speaking of November — I want to organize a Diwali potluck for the club! I'll teach everyone to make murukku, a crunchy South Indian snack.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Two November celebrations? I'm in for both.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: Me too. Things have been going great at Kura lately. Being the head sushi chef at a restaurant in the Warehouse District keeps me busy, but I always make time for Wednesdays.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: That's what this club is about. Speaking of big news — I've been meaning to tell everyone about my trip to Lyon last February. Three weeks training under Chef Michel Girard at a Michelin-starred restaurant.

turns.speaker: lorraine
turns.text: Three weeks in France? Baby, why didn't you tell us sooner?

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: I was waiting for the right time. He taught me things about sauce-making that I've been incorporating into the Bayou Table menu.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: So it's settled? Dia de los Muertos and Diwali in November, holiday sale in December?

turns.speaker: priya
turns.text: And the three-hundred-tamale marathon for Second Harvest.

turns.speaker: rosa
turns.text: Don't remind me. My hands are already hurting thinking about it.

turns.speaker: hideo
turns.text: I'll help with the rolling this year. My sushi-rolling skills should transfer.

turns.speaker: marcus
turns.text: That's the spirit. This club is the best thing I've ever created.
